topics.summary: Both endings make the noun das and usually add an umlaut.

explanation.heading: Always das
explanation.text: Nouns ending in -chen or -lein take the das article, whatever the gender of the original noun: der Rock → das Röckchen.

explanation.heading: Meaning
explanation.text: The ending -chen / -lein means something is small; -chen also means something is nice or attractive.

rules: -chen and -lein always make the noun neuter: das Röckchen, das Jäckchen.
There is usually a vowel change: a → ä, o → ö, u → ü.
The ending marks smallness; -chen can also add a friendly, attractive tone.

exercises.prompt: Which article does a noun in -chen take?
exercises.explain: -chen and -lein always make the noun neuter.

exercises.prompt: Form the diminutive of die Jacke.
exercises.explain: a → ä plus -chen, and the article becomes das.

exercises.prompt: Complete the vowel change.
exercises.explain: o → ö is the usual change before -chen.

exercises.prompt: What does the ending -chen express?
exercises.explain: It marks smallness, and with -chen often a nice or attractive tone.

topics.summary: Only the masculine changes: der → den. Everything else stays the same.

explanation.heading: One change only
explanation.text: Between the nominative and the accusative, only the masculine article changes: der becomes den. Neuter, feminine and plural keep the same form.

rules: Nominative: der Computer, das Telefon, die Kamera, die Kassetten.
Accusative: den Computer, das Telefon, die Kamera, die Kassetten.
So the only difference is masculine der → den.

exercises.prompt: Accusative of der Computer.
exercises.explain: Masculine der becomes den in the accusative.

exercises.prompt: Which article changes between nominative and accusative?
exercises.explain: Only der → den; the others stay the same.

exercises.prompt: Accusative of die Kamera.
exercises.explain: The feminine article is die in both cases.

exercises.prompt: The article is wrong in the accusative. Correct it.
exercises.explain: brauchen takes the accusative, so der becomes den.

topics.titleEn: Indefinite and negative articles: nominative and accusative
topics.summary: ein/kein behave alike; only the masculine accusative adds -en.

explanation.heading: Same endings
explanation.text: The negative article kein takes exactly the same endings as the indefinite article ein. The only change between nominative and accusative is again in the masculine.

explanation.heading: No plural of ein
explanation.text: ein has no plural form, so the plural shows only kein: keine Kassetten.

rules: Nominative masculine: ein / kein Computer. Accusative masculine: einen / keinen Computer.
Neuter: ein / kein Telefon in both cases.
Feminine: eine / keine Kamera in both cases.
Plural: no ein, only keine Kassetten.

exercises.prompt: Masculine accusative of ein.
exercises.explain: Masculine accusative adds -en: einen.

exercises.prompt: Which is the plural of ein?
exercises.explain: ein has no plural; only kein appears in the plural.

exercises.prompt: Negative article, feminine accusative.
exercises.explain: Feminine keine is the same in nominative and accusative.

exercises.prompt: The masculine accusative needs an ending. Correct it.
exercises.explain: Masculine accusative: keinen.

topics.titleEn: Definite article: nominative, accusative and dative
topics.summary: Adds the dative — dem, dem, der, den — and the -n on the dative plural.

explanation.heading: The dative row
explanation.text: In the dative the articles are dem (masculine), dem (neuter), der (feminine) and den (plural).

explanation.heading: The dative plural -n
explanation.text: In the dative plural the noun itself takes an extra -n: den Söhnen, den Kindern, den Töchtern. Nouns whose plural already ends in -s do not: den T-Shirts, den Festivals, den Autos.

rules: Nom.: der Sohn, das Kind, die Tochter, die Söhne.
Akk.: den Sohn, das Kind, die Tochter, die Söhne.
Dat.: dem Sohn, dem Kind, der Tochter, den Söhnen.
The dative plural noun adds -n, except for plurals in -s.

examples.de: den Söhne n / Kinder n / Töchter n

exercises.prompt: Feminine dative article.
exercises.explain: The feminine dative is der — the same form as the masculine nominative.

exercises.prompt: Dative plural — mind the noun ending.
exercises.explain: The dative plural noun takes an extra -n.

exercises.prompt: Which dative plural takes NO extra -n?
exercises.explain: Plurals ending in -s do not add another -n.

exercises.prompt: The dative plural is missing its -n. Correct it.
exercises.text: Ich gebe den Kinder ein Buch.
answers: Ich gebe den Kindern ein Buch.
exercises.explain: The dative plural noun adds -n: den Kindern.

topics.titleEn: Indefinite, negative and possessive articles: all three cases
topics.summary: ein, kein and mein share one set of endings across nominative, accusative and dative.

explanation.heading: One pattern, three words
explanation.text: ein, kein and mein all decline the same way, so learning one gives you all of them — and the same endings carry over to dein, sein, ihr, unser and euer.

explanation.heading: The dative
explanation.text: The dative endings are -em (masculine and neuter), -er (feminine) and -en (plural), with the extra -n on the plural noun.

rules: Nom.: ein / kein / mein Sohn, ein Kind, eine Tochter, keine / meine Söhne.
Akk.: einen / keinen / meinen Sohn; neuter and feminine unchanged.
Dat.: einem / keinem / meinem Sohn, einem Kind, einer / keiner / meiner Tochter.
Dative plural: keinen / meinen Söhnen — article in -en and noun in -n.

examples.de: ein en / kein en / mein en
ein em / kein em / mein em
eine r / keine r / meine r
- / kein en / mein en Söhne n /

exercises.prompt: Masculine dative of mein.
exercises.explain: Masculine dative takes -em: meinem.

exercises.prompt: Feminine dative of kein.
exercises.explain: Feminine dative takes -er: keiner.

exercises.prompt: Which words share this same set of endings?
exercises.explain: The endings on possessive articles are the same as the indefinite and the negative article.

exercises.prompt: Both the article and the noun need a dative-plural ending. Correct it.
exercises.text: Ich schreibe meine Söhne eine E-Mail.
answers: Ich schreibe meinen Söhnen eine E-Mail.
exercises.explain: Dative plural: meinen Söhnen.

topics.summary: Some masculine nouns add -(e)n in every case except the nominative singular.

explanation.heading: The one exception
explanation.text: A group of masculine nouns whose plural ends in -(e)n take that same -(e)n in the accusative and dative singular too. Only the nominative singular is without it.

rules: Nominative singular: der Herr, der Nachbar, der Kollege — no ending.
Accusative and dative singular: den/dem Herrn, Nachbarn, Kollegen.
All plural forms: die Herren, Nachbarn, Kollegen.
So the bare form appears only once, in the nominative singular.

examples.de: den / einen Herr n / Nachbar n / Kollege n
mit dem / einem Herr n / Nachbar n / Kollege n
die / - Herr en / Nachbar n / Kollege n

exercises.prompt: Accusative singular of der Nachbar.
exercises.explain: n-declension nouns add -n outside the nominative singular.

exercises.prompt: Dative singular of der Kollege.
exercises.explain: The dative singular also takes the -n.

exercises.prompt: In which case does the n-declension noun have NO ending?
exercises.explain: Only the nominative singular is the bare form.

exercises.prompt: This noun follows the n-declension. Correct it.
exercises.text: Ich habe den Herr gestern getroffen.
answers: Ich habe den Herrn gestern getroffen.
exercises.explain: Accusative singular: den Herrn.
